Chapter Six: The Contest Years—A Mother’s Secret World
You know that gentle hush that settles over the house late at night—when the kids are finally asleep, and the world outside fades into quiet?
That’s when the mother’s world shrinks down to just her, the kitchen table, a battered old dictionary, and a pile of contest entry forms.
This is her time—her own hidden little world—where she gets to be more than just a caretaker or a wife. Here, she’s a wordsmith. She’s a strategist. She’s a dreamer.
Most people never really see what goes into one of her entries. She’ll pore over product labels, hunting for the tiniest spark of inspiration. Maybe she’ll whisper a rhyme under her breath, scribbling out drafts and, sometimes, crumpling up a page when it just doesn’t work. There’s a rhythm to her routine—the hope that comes with each fresh contest, the nerves of waiting, the thrill when she wins, and, of course, the sting of rejection.
But she keeps at it, night after night, because every entry is another chance—a small but powerful rebellion against the limits of her everyday life.
Every now and then, a child might wake up in the night and spot her at the table, head bowed in deep concentration. They notice how her face lights up when she lands on the perfect phrase, or how she quietly tucks away her disappointment when a letter brings bad news. The kids might not totally get what’s at stake, but they can sense that this work means something.
And over time, her contest wins become the stuff of family legend.
Remember when that shiny new freezer arrived, and the kids gathered around it, eyes wide? Or the day a year’s supply of groceries showed up at the door—turning a tough month into a celebration?
Each prize is more than just a reward—it’s proof that their mother’s words have real power. Her creativity can put food on the table, and hope in everyone’s heart.
But, honestly, these contest years are about so much more than the prizes.
They’re about her determination to carve out her own space, to prove she’s more than just the sum of her struggles. In a world that often looks right past women like her, she finds a way to be seen, to feel valued, to make a difference.
Most folks don’t realize just how much courage it takes to keep going—to keep believing that your words matter.
For this mother, every contest is a chance to claim her own worth.
